claim: LLM judges exhibit strong position bias in pairwise evaluation: simply swapping the order of two responses changes the verdict for a large fraction of items (GPT-4 conflict rate 46.3% for Vicuna-13B vs ChatGPT; ChatGPT judge 82.5%), enough to flip which model 'wins', even when the prompt tells the judge to ignore order.

paper.title: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
paper.citation_source: Semantic Scholar Graph API POST https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/batch?fields=title,citationCount,publicationDate,externalIds,venue (id arXiv:2305.17926)
paper.s2_batch_record_title: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators

experiment.location_in_paper: Section 2.2, Table 1 (template), Table 2, Figure 2; Section 4, Table 4
experiment.task_or_benchmark: Vicuna Benchmark, 80 questions in 9 categories; response pairs Vicuna-13B vs ChatGPT and Vicuna-13B vs Alpaca-13B.
experiment.intervention_or_prompts: Vicuna/Zheng et al. scoring template asking for two 1-10 scores with explicit instruction 'ensuring that the order in which the responses were presented does not affect your judgment'; each pair queried twice with positions swapped. Calibrations: Multiple Evidence Calibration (explain-then-score, k samples), Balanced Position Calibration (average both orders), Human-in-the-loop via entropy.
experiment.evaluation_procedure: Conflict rate = share of items whose verdict differs between the two orders; win rate of Vicuna-13B when placed as Assistant 1 vs 2. For calibration: accuracy and kappa against majority of 3 author annotators (win/tie/lose). Temperature 0 for vanilla, 1 with k=3 for MEC; non-BPC methods averaged over 100 random orderings.
experiment.metric: Conflict rate; win rate by position; accuracy/kappa vs human majority
experiment.main_comparison: Same judge, same pair, response order swapped
experiment.main_result: GPT-4 judge: Vicuna-13B win rate 51.3% as Assistant 1 vs 23.8% as Assistant 2, conflict 37/80 (46.3%); vs Alpaca 5.0% conflict. ChatGPT judge: 2.5% vs 82.5% win rate, conflict 66/80 (82.5%); vs Alpaca 52.5%. GPT-4 favors first position, ChatGPT second. Conflicts concentrate where score gap <=1. Vanilla GPT-4 accuracy vs humans 52.7% (kappa 0.24) -> 62.5% with MEC+BPC; ChatGPT 44.4% -> 58.7%; human annotators average 71.7%.

downstream.title: Judging the Judges: A Systematic Study of Position Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
downstream.summary: 15 judges on MT-Bench and DevBench: position bias persists and is not random (repetition stability >0.95 for Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4, Llama-3.3-70B), direction varies by task (e.g. Claude-3.5-Sonnet near-fair on MT-Bench, PF=0.01, but recency-biased on DevBench, PF=0.22); bias largest when answer quality gap is small (read abstract, Sec. results L62-65).

downstream.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
downstream.summary: Concurrent: on near-identical GPT-3.5 answer pairs, only GPT-4 is position-consistent in >60% of cases (65%); Claude-v1 75% biased toward first slot (Table 2).

downstream.title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
downstream.summary: GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 reverse pairwise preferences on order swap at 25%, 58% and 89% of summarization pairs.

downstream.title: Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge (CALM)
downstream.summary: Position bias tested among 12 biases on 2024 judges (GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5, etc.); robustness improves with capability but judges remain order-sensitive, especially with more than two candidates (abstract + Fig 6 caption read).

downstream_summary: Position bias is one of the most replicated LLM-judge findings; newer, stronger judges are more consistent than ChatGPT-era judges but still show systematic, task-dependent order effects, especially for close pairs.
notability_notes: Canonical position-bias paper for LLM evaluators; 1.3k citations; its balanced-position calibration became standard practice.
gaps: Only 80 questions and 2 pairings; the 'gpt-4' alias snapshot is unspecified. Human ground truth from 3 authors only.
